examples.knowledge_point: Computing the Limit at Infinity of a Constant Function
examples.worked_solution:
When we divide the two functions, we get a constant, and the limit of a constant is just the constant itself:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -\infty }\frac{p(x)}{q(x)} & ={lim}_{x\to -\infty }\frac{9{x}^{4}}{3{x}^{4}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to -\infty }3 \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.worked_solution:
First, we note that

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -\infty }5{x}^{3} & ={lim}_{x\to -\infty }(5\cdot {x}^{3}) \\  & =5\cdot {lim}_{x\to -\infty }{x}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

The graph $y={x}^{3}$ is power function with an odd positive power and therefore has the property that

$$
{lim}_{x\to -\infty }{x}^{3}=-\infty .
$$

Multiplication by the positive constant $5$ does not affect the limit at infinity. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned} & =5\cdot {lim}_{x\to -\infty }{x}^{3} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to -\infty }{x}^{3} \\  & =-\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
{lim}_{x\to -\infty }(5{x}^{3})=-\infty .
$$
